title: DO JOB TITLES REALLY MATTER?
subtitle: Read the text again and think of one word which best fits each space (1–8). Use only one word in each space. There is an example at the beginning (0).
passage:
In a (0) WORD, yes. Within an organisation, a person's job title can clarify an employee's role and status. Outside of work, it is often brandished as a marker of one's self-identity, a prism through which we present ourselves to the world. As [[1]], these titles should be chosen with care.

Sadly, this is not always the [[2]]. Many companies today are succumbing [[3]] the temptation of job title inflation. This is the practice of levelling [[4]] an employee's job title without increasing their responsibilities (or salary) – for instance, adding 'Senior' in front of a 'Software Engineer' position with junior requirements.

On the [[5]] of it, job title inflation might seem like a tempting way to soften the [[6]] when you can't give an employee their desired pay rise or promotion, but it is ultimately detrimental. [[7]] loftier titles be bestowed upon employees at random, it can breed resentment among others doing similar work. Even worse, inflated titles create undue confusion, defeating the [[8]] of having a job title in the first place: to tell people who you are and what you do.

explanations.1: As such means ‘for that reason’ or ‘therefore’ — the titles matter, so they should be chosen carefully.
explanations.2: Not always the case — a fixed phrase meaning ‘not always true in practice’.
explanations.3: Succumb to — the verb collocates with to before the temptation.
explanations.4: Level up — inflate or upgrade the title without changing the role.
explanations.5: On the face of it — at first glance; apparently.
explanations.6: Soften the blow — make bad news (no pay rise) feel less harsh.
explanations.7: Should + subject + base verb — inverted conditional: ‘If loftier titles are bestowed…’.
explanations.8: Defeating the purpose — the reason for having titles in the first place.
